summary: Registers the application/xhtml+xml MIME media type for XHTML-based markup. It does not replace the text/html registration. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Every file on the web has a label saying what kind it is. This creates the label for a stricter kind of web page called XHTML.

subtitle: Registers the MIME type for XML-based web pages following HTML rules.

tldr.problem: XHTML is HTML reformulated in XML, so it needs its own MIME media type to distinguish it from plain HTML and to signal that user agents should treat it as XML rather than forgiving HTML.
tldr.mechanism: This memo registers application/xhtml+xml as the official MIME type for XHTML documents, with parameters for charset and for indicating which XHTML variant is in use.
tldr.outcome: Web servers, browsers, and proxy servers can now negotiate and deliver XHTML with the correct media type, and developers have a standard way to serve stricty XML-based markup.

today: RFC 3236 is informational and remains the official MIME type registration for XHTML. However, in practice, most XHTML documents on the web were served as text/html for compatibility with browsers. XHTML2 work was discontinued in 2009. HTML5 is now the dominant standard for web markup, and it is not XML-based, though XHTML5 variants exist. Modern XML-based markup often uses specific formats like SVG or XML directly rather than XHTML.

sections.title: XHTML and the Need for a New Type
sections.content:
In 1998, the W3C HTML Working Group began rewriting HTML as an XML application. HTML had its own lenient syntax: browsers ignore typos and unrecognized tags. XML is strict: a single typo breaks the document.

XHTML 1.0, published in January 2000, is HTML 4.01 rewritten in XML syntax. It lets developers use familiar HTML elements while following XML rules. But the old media type text/html signals that the document is forgiving HTML, not strict XML. A separate type was needed to tell user agents that XHTML should be parsed as XML.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to write a web page: the loose, flexible HTML way, or the strict XML way. XHTML uses XML rules with HTML elements. A new label tells browsers which one it is.

sections.title: The Media Type Registration
sections.content:
RFC 3236 formally registers the MIME type application/xhtml+xml. It is an application type (not text), and the +xml suffix, following the convention in RFC 3023, signals that the document conforms to XML syntax. There are no required parameters.

Two optional parameters are defined. The charset parameter works the same as for application/xml: it specifies the text encoding (default UTF-8). The profile parameter lets a sender indicate which XHTML variant is in use, using a URI such as http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml-basic/xhtml-basic10.dtd. This lets proxies and user agents check if they support the variant before processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The official label for XHTML is application/xhtml+xml. You can add optional tags to say what encoding it uses and which kind of XHTML it is.

sections.title: Recognizing XHTML Files
sections.content:
XHTML files begin with an XML declaration (optional) such as <?xml version="1.0"?>, followed by an XHTML document type declaration listing the XHTML DTD. All conforming XHTML 1.0 documents include the HTML namespace declaration xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" and the root element <html>.

File extensions for XHTML are .xhtml, .xht, or .html. (Using .html can confuse web servers into serving the file as text/html instead of application/xhtml+xml, so .xhtml is preferred.) There is no reliable magic number for XHTML files, but the presence of the XHTML namespace declaration is a strong indicator.
sections.plainLanguage: XHTML files start with <?xml>, have a DOCTYPE, declare the XHTML namespace, and use .xhtml extension (though some use .html).

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers and Encoding
sections.content:
XHTML inherits XML's fragment identifier semantics: an anchor like #foo points to the element with id="foo", not name="foo" as in HTML. This follows XML Pointer conventions.

XHTML documents sent as application/xhtml+xml use XML encoding rules. The charset parameter defaults to UTF-8 but can specify other XML encodings. The XML declaration can override the charset if present.
sections.plainLanguage: In XHTML, #anchor works like in XML, pointing to id attributes. The encoding rules are the same as XML.

sections.title: Security and Extensibility
sections.content: The security considerations for XHTML follow those for HTML (RFC 2854) and XML (RFC 3023): scripts and embedded objects can be dangerous, and content from untrusted sources must be validated. A key difference is that XHTML Modularization lets developers create XHTML-based languages with additional elements beyond the base XHTML 1.0 set. If a browser encounters unknown elements, it should ignore them per XHTML conformance rules. But if the browser recognizes and processes unknown extensions, security risks can arise. User agents should only process extensions they explicitly support.
sections.plainLanguage: XHTML can be extended with custom elements. Browsers ignore unknown ones by default, which is safe. But if a browser recognizes an extension, it might have security risks, so be careful with untrusted content.
